paragraphs: In the fifth month of the twenty-third year of Jianyuan, just as the wheat in Hebei was coming into ear, the rains began.

At first the farmers outside Ye laughed. Spring had been dry, they said; a soaking rain was exactly what they had prayed for. On the first night, jars beneath the eaves filled to the brim, and barefoot children chased floating leaves down the muddy lanes. By the third day, field ridges had collapsed and the ears of wheat lay in the mud. By the sixth, the waters of the Zhang River had turned from green to yellow, so yellow it was as though someone had scooped an entire wasteland from the riverbed.

East of Anyang, an old farmer noticed fine red earth from upstream floating in the flood and urged the county military officer guarding the embankment to move people to higher ground. The officer said the upstream districts had reported safety only the day before and warned him not to spread alarm. Under cover of darkness the old man drove his two oxen uphill and led away a grain cart for his widowed neighbor. In the middle of the night the embankment finally gave way.

The breach was at first no wider than an arm. Soldiers stuffed in sacks of grass, only to see them instantly swept away. A village head rode off to carry word, when a crack like muffled thunder sounded behind him. Looking back, he saw a wall of muddy yellow water crashing toward him with roof beams, sheaves of wheat, and dark shapes of livestock caught in its rush. Torches went out one after another. He did not look back again, but lay flat across his horse and rode for his life. Only at dawn did he learn that his village no longer stood where it had been.

On the riverbank a woman climbed into the branches of a surviving mulberry tree and held her child until sunrise. A lacquered clothing chest drifted past beneath her, its lid open. Red silk embroidered with mandarin ducks turned twice in the current and suddenly sank. The child asked where their house had gone. She pointed at the water, moved her lips several times, and could say nothing.

Within three days more than ten counties along the Zhang and Huan rivers sent appeals for help. The first county reports counted ruined fields in the thousands of qing; later reports spoke of tens of thousands made homeless. After that, some county seats could no longer muster even a horse to carry messages. The most urgent dispatch contained only a few words: Embankments entirely broken. Water all around the town. The living and dead not yet counted.

One night watchers on Ye’s northern tower saw a broad field of lights floating above the distant lowlands. At first they thought houses still stood in the flooded villages. Later they learned that the refugees had tied door panels together into rafts and were drifting with oil lamps held high. More and more lights gathered until, far away, they looked like a second river of stars running across the earth.
On the eleventh night of rain, the first military dispatch about the flood reached Chang’an.

The lamps in the Secretariat burned through the night. When a second map was unrolled, even that could not contain all the red marks. The grain figures reported by the commanderies contradicted one another. Ye’s ever-normal granary recorded 120,000 shi, but 30,000 shi had gone moldy in the damp. The military stores held 190,000 shi, but the garrison needed its provisions until autumn, and emergency transfers could not leave the city guards without food. Grain could be gathered in neighboring Henei and Shangdang, but the roads were flooded: the fastest delivery to Ye would take at least half a month.
Fu Hong asked the granary officer, “How many days can those in the shelters eat on what we have now?”
“Eleven days, according to yesterday’s count. That excludes new arrivals.”
“And the boats?”
“Most civilian boats have been requisitioned upstream. The counties don’t have enough left for three days of round trips.”

A Household Office clerk proposed checking each refugee’s Qin registration before issuing grain by household. Many had drifted in from commanderies of the old Yan, he explained, where names and registers were confused. Without checks, powerful families would pass their retainers off as refugees and take extra rations. Fu Hong told him to bring the map of Heshuo and asked where the county offices in the disaster zone stood. The clerk pointed out more than ten sites; red flood lines cut across several of them.
“Which county hall will you go to today to check their registrations?” the Crown Prince asked.
The clerk lowered his head.

Fu Hong set down his brush. “First check the boat journeys and the granary totals, then distribute the grain through the shelters. Write down names for anyone willing to give them. Give life-saving porridge first even to those who will not. Mark those served by wooden tokens and shelter numbers, and verify them again in two days. Punish fraud if you find it later. Don’t make children stand in floodwater waiting for a piece of paper already soaked to pulp.”

Another official proposed transferring a hundred thousand refugees to reclaim land in Hexi, arguing that there was plenty of waste ground and such a move would solve the problem for good. Fu Rong asked who would hold their original fields after the waters receded if all those people left. The official replied that the scale of the disaster was uncertain and required a long view. Fu Rong shook his head. The beams of their houses were still floating in the river, he said. Surely it was too soon to find them new doorways elsewhere.

Fu Hong ordered Ye’s ever-normal granary opened, an initial release of 50,000 shi from the military stores, and follow-up shipments from Henei. Counties could temporarily requisition boats, carts, and empty houses, but had to record their owners and pay fair compensation afterward. No one might seize land deeds under cover of the flood or conscript displaced people into private retainers' bands. Separate registers were to be kept for disease prevention and burials. Grain-boat accounts were to be reconciled every ten days; in the hardest-hit districts no verification of households was to delay rescue.
But when the court came to choose who would command the relief effort, discussion stalled.

The waterways of Hebei were unpredictable, and bridges between the commanderies had been swept away. An ordinary provincial inspector could command only his own jurisdiction; the people of former Yan might not obey even a seasoned prince of the Qin clan. Some proposed Fu Pi, but he was still stationed in the southern command. By the time he transferred north, the few days most vital for rescue would be gone. Fu Rong thought for a long time and then spoke the name Murong Chui.

Voices in the hall immediately objected. The old homeland of the Murong clan lay around Ye. Though Former Yan had fallen twenty years ago, old seals of the Yan palace could still be found hidden in the garrisons. If Murong Chui were entrusted with thirty thousand soldiers, the grain stores of several commanderies, and their river crossings, what would become of the precautions the court had maintained for years?

Fu Hong did not rebuke them. He remembered what Wang Meng had said on his sickbed, but also how Murong Chui had commanded at Guzang and Wei Bridge. He opened the central army’s muster roll himself. “When we say thirty thousand can be assigned, do we mean thirty thousand can arrive immediately, or that units along the route will come under his tally one by one?”

The central army office replied that Murong Chui could set out that very night with five hundred light cavalry. Troops from Henei, Wei Commandery, and the river garrisons could gradually be placed under an auxiliary central command tally for flood relief; gathering all thirty thousand would take more than ten days, and frontier guards must not be withdrawn without permission. Fu Hong ordered the distinction written into the edict. Otherwise a number carried to the provinces would become, in the telling, thirty thousand men already standing at the gates.
At last Fu Jian said, “Send him.”

Fu Hong turned toward his father. Fu Jian had already passed the seal of the disaster-relief commissioner to the Secretariat. He did not say, “I trust him.” The seal was not heavy, yet when it touched the table several of the protesting ministers fell silent.

The edict authorized Murong Chui to coordinate temporary relief forces, open granaries, requisition boats and carts, oversee the waterways, and act against negligent county officials. Matters involving governors or provincial inspectors and above must be reported to Chang’an. He might neither appoint governors on his own authority nor recruit a private army; personnel, grain, and boat registers were to be submitted every ten days. The Crown Prince appointed Censor Pei Heng to accompany him. At the end of the document Fu Hong added a line: emergency measures could be taken first, but their actual costs and the people rescued must be verified afterward. There would then be evidence if the Court of Justice ever needed to assign responsibility.
That night Murong Chui was repairing an old bow from Yan in his house.

A thin crack ran across its back. A craftsman had said it would break if drawn again, but he would not replace it. He wound ox sinew around it a strand at a time. When the messenger entered the courtyard, lamplight fell on the old bow; the lacquer had worn from the tips. Murong Chui heard his orders and commanded that horses be made ready. His wife stood under the corridor and asked whether Ye would still know him.
“Some people will.”
“Why are you going back?”
“To save people from the flood.”
After a long silence she said, “It was your home once.”
Murong Chui returned the bow to its rack. “The people there may not even have roofs over their heads now.”

As he left Chang’an, Fu Rong rode after him to Ba Bridge. The night rain was so thick the river could barely be seen; only the horses' breath rose white above the bridge. Fu Rong handed him the deputy tally of the central army and warned him to watch the former Yan ministers, lest they exploit the disaster to gather their old retainers again. Murong Chui asked, “Are you afraid I’ll go home and cease to recognize Chang’an?”
“I’m afraid someone will recognize you and forget what duty he has now.”
“And if I recognize them?”
“Then save them first.”
Murong Chui took the tally and mounted. Behind him Fu Rong called again, “Daoxuan!”
Murong Chui checked his reins.
“Don’t let ordinary people have to trade the name of their lost country for a bag of grain.”
The wind tore the latter part of the sentence apart, but Murong Chui heard every word.

Several hundred li eastward, the roads filled with more and more refugees. Many walked west carrying children on their backs and bundles over their shoulders, turning now and then to look behind. Broken timbers swept downriver still struck the bridge piers with a sound that made them afraid to look back. The magistrate of Hongnong refused to open his granary: these were not households registered in his county, he argued, and its grain must feed its own people until autumn. Murong Chui produced the relief commissioner’s seal and ordered three days' rations issued first, with the balance to be audited and replenished by Chang’an afterward.

People pressed against people before the granary. A soldier drew his sword and shouted at a woman who had pushed through to the door. Murong Chui ordered him to sheathe it, shifted a section of the wooden barrier aside himself, and had the grain taken out through the rear gate. Those who received their portion could leave without colliding with those still waiting. Within half an hour the crowd had begun to form a line.

Under the eaves Pei Heng kept the accounts. Seeing that the granary clerks were not checking each household’s registration, he asked how the general would reconcile the figures later. Murong Chui told him to record traffic through the granary gates, the number of sacks, and the sequence of wooden tokens. Still uneasy, Pei Heng ordered holes punched in each token on the spot so the next county could inspect the holes before issuing further rations. Murong Chui studied him for a moment, then laughed. “I doubt you’ll ever trust another soul in your life.”
“My commission is to keep the accounts,” said Pei Heng.
“Then keep them.”
“The order to open the granary came from you personally, General. If the figures fail to agree afterward, I will report that too.”
“Write that down as well.”

One watched the people at the granary gate and the other checked the figures beneath the eaves; they worked together with surprising ease. Near dusk, a woman recognized Murong Chui’s face and asked whether he was the former Prince of Wu of Yan. She had once washed horses' manes in his household at Ye. Several people nearby turned toward them.
Murong Chui helped lift a grain sack onto her son’s cart. “The man who can open this granary for you today,” he answered, “is a Qin disaster-relief commissioner.”
She stared at him. “I was asking about before.”
Murong Chui steadied the cart shaft. “There was no flood like this before,” he said quietly.
Her child helped her away, but she kept looking back. Pei Heng’s brush paused for an instant and then went on writing.

In Henei, the master of a fortified estate led three hundred tenant farmers northward. He said the village fields had flooded and he wanted to take his people to Shangdang for shelter. Pei Heng investigated and found that most households still had their land, but the deeds were all locked inside the estate. An elderly woman wept publicly that she did not want to leave her home. A strong farmer insisted he did want to go, because the master had grain and oxen and the government had not yet delivered seed.

Murong Chui did not order his soldiers to drag everyone back. He separated those who wished to leave from those who wished to stay and had county clerks record each person’s name. Those leaving received temporary travel papers; their land would not be confiscated merely because they departed, and copies of their old debts would remain with the county so the estate owner could not add another charge along the road. The master’s face darkened as he watched Pei Heng seal the papers, as though he had been cut by a blade. But the tenant asked, “General, if we go beyond Shangdang, will we ever be able to return home?”
“The road will still be there,” Murong Chui said. “If anyone bars it, bring your papers back and complain.”

He knew it was easier to say than to carry out. By the time the farmers returned, canals and boundaries might have changed. He therefore ordered local soldiers to record the positions of the old mulberry tree at the village entrance and the graveyard, so people coming home would have something they could recognize.

Farther ahead, more than a thousand people were stranded across a broken bridge. Nearby, the Han family’s fortified estate stood on a rise, with more than ten flat-bottomed boats moored inside its walls. The magistrate had asked to borrow them, but the family refused: the boats were the only escape route for the eight hundred people of its estate. Murong Chui intended to requisition them. The estate master climbed onto the wall and demanded written proof, asking who could believe the promise of compensation for these boats when debts from the southern campaign had still not been paid.
“If you won’t lend the boats, people will die!” Murong Chui called up.
“My family must live too!” came the answer from the wall.

Pei Heng held the general back for a moment. He ordered county clerks to record the condition, construction, and assessed value of every boat. The commissioner, censor, and county office were to sign jointly; one copy of each official voucher would be kept by the owner and one by the office, stating the period of requisition and the bureau responsible for repayment. The estate master read the papers several times and finally opened his gate. As the boats were launched, an old man on one of them bowed his head toward the estate in thanks. A government soldier moved to correct him, but Murong Chui stopped him. “It was a Han family boat that carried him to safety. Let him thank them.”

Pei Heng heard this and entered only the facts in his daily log: fifteen boats requisitioned; first crossing, 147 persons; the Han family temporarily holding official compensation vouchers. He also recorded, without omission, that earlier that day the general had nearly ordered his troops to storm the estate.

The day before reaching Ye, the rain thinned. The northern light was pale, and the muddy water reflected broken field ridges like a bronze mirror smashed to pieces. At the distant sight of the city wall, Murong Chui halted his horse. More than ten years before he had passed through these gates countless times; now most of the graves, houses, and old trees beyond them were scarcely recognizable.

The city’s grain officer reported that the official stores could feed the present population for only eleven days. More than eighty thousand refugees were inside and outside the walls, not counting the missing. Murong Chui first ordered porridge shelters erected, mud cleared, and breaches in the embankments inspected. The dead were to be recorded where found, with wooden tags noting clothing, age, and location. No corpse was to be cast aside merely because no Qin household record could be located.
As the city gate opened, a white-haired old man suddenly dropped to his knees in the rain.
“The Prince of Wu has come back!”

The cry rang through muddy streets. Several former Yan soldiers knelt as well; some wept, others started in alarm. Most of the younger people only exchanged uncertain glances. They had heard that Yan once had a Prince of Wu, but had never seen him. Beside the horse Pei Heng tightened his grip on his writing brush. The escorting soldiers instinctively reached toward their swords.

Murong Chui dismounted and went to the old man. The fellow had once tended horses for the household of the Prince of Wu, and his arm still bore an old break from the kick of a vicious mount. He called him “Your Highness” through a face wet with tears, forgetting that he knelt in deep mud.
Murong Chui bent to help him rise. After a long pause he said, “Stand up. Three granaries will open in Ye tonight. Send your family to collect food first.”
“Your Highness will still look after us?”
“I will.”
“Then you’ve come back to—”

Murong Chui did not let him finish. He took out the relief commissioner’s seal and handed it to the gate officer, instructing him to announce the granary locations, boat crossings, and embankment repair sites in the street. The old veterans of Yan listened, their eyes slowly losing some of their light. Someone behind them muttered that the Prince of Wu no longer acknowledged Yan; another cursed those who cared only for old banners while children were still drowning in the flood.

Before dark all three granaries had indeed opened. Thousands stood in line for porridge in the north of the city, and the boat crews west of the walls rescued more than seven hundred people still trapped by the water. Murong Chui inspected the embankments along the city wall. On his return Pei Heng handed him the day’s accounts and drew an old wooden tablet from his sleeve. The front carried a design from the gates of the Former Yan palace; four characters had been freshly cut on its back: Former servants await you.
“Where did this come from?” Murong Chui asked.
“Someone passed it to an old official of Ye, asking him to come to the site of the former Yan palace tonight.”

The old palace stood on high ground east of the city, still untouched by the flood. Murong Chui looked toward it. Its walls lay deep in darkness; only one point of lamplight showed beneath the sweeping eaves. Pei Heng asked if the men should be arrested immediately. Murong Chui shook his head.
“The rescue boats are still on the river tonight. Watch the gates first, and record everyone who enters or leaves.”
“Will you go, General?”
Murong Chui slipped the old wooden tablet into his sleeve. Rain had chilled the cuff against his wrist.
“Old acquaintances have invited me,” he said. “I must at least learn what they intend to bring to our meeting now.”

Pei Heng looked at him as if he might offer advice. In the end he merely entered the words in the day’s register. The bell tower of Ye’s old palace had stood silent for years. Tonight someone struck a bronze chime there. Its single note traveled across the wet, dark streets to the porridge shelters newly lit throughout the city.
